title: Electric Potential
notes: Electric potential at a point is the work done by an external agent, without changing kinetic energy, in bringing a unit positive charge from infinity to that point. It is a scalar. The unit is the volt.
A point charge Q gives V = k Q / r. A positive charge makes a positive potential. There is no direction to add, so potentials from several charges add as ordinary numbers.
The potential difference between two points is the work per unit charge to move a test charge between them. A charge q changes its potential energy by q ΔV.
Equipotential surfaces join points of equal potential. The field is perpendicular to an equipotential. No work is done moving a charge on an equipotential.
In a uniform field the potential falls along the field direction. Between plates, E = V/d if V is the potential difference and d is the separation, in the uniform region.
Potential can be zero where the field is not, as at the midpoint between equal and opposite charges. The two scalars cancel, but the two field vectors point the same way.
confusion: ❌ 'Electric potential is the same as electric potential energy.' ✅ Potential is *energy per unit charge* (J/C); potential energy is the *total energy* (J) required to assemble charges.
❌ 'Electric potential is zero where the electric field is zero.' ✅ Not always true (e.g., at the center of a charged ring, E=0 but V≠0).
❌ 'Electric potential is a vector quantity.' ✅ It is a *scalar* quantity; it has magnitude but no direction, though it can be positive or negative.
Zero potential does not mean zero field.
A negative charge is attracted toward higher potential.
Work on an equipotential is zero.
